column1: Coupled criticality analysis of inflation and unemployment

The thesis titled Coupled Criticality Analysis of Inflation and Unemployment by Z. Koohi Lai  A. Namaki  A. Hosseiny  G.R. Jafari  and M. Ausloos  published on arXiv  explores the complex relationship between inflation and unemployment through a coupled multifractal approach. The study focuses on the critical periods in the economy characterized by significant fluctuations in macroeconomic indicators  specifically inflation and unemployment. The authors aim to capture these unusual and large fluctuations by examining the non-Gaussianity of their distributions over a 70-year period of US data from 1948 to 2018.

The research employs a multifractal random walk (MRW) model to analyze the time series data  which is useful for presenting the non-Gaussian behavior of economic indicators. The MRW model is composed of the product of two processes with normal and log-normal probability density functions (PDFs). The variance of the log-normal part determines the strength of non-Gaussianity in the original signal. The study finds that the non-Gaussianity of unemployment is noticeable only for periods shorter than one year  tending towards Gaussian behavior for longer periods. In contrast  the non-Gaussianity of inflation persists across all time scales. Additionally  the coupling structure of these variables tends to exhibit Gaussian behavior after two years.

The authors further apply the bivariate Multifractal Random Walk (Bi-MRW) method to analyze the joint non-Gaussian stochastic processes of inflation and unemployment. This approach allows for the examination of cross-correlations between large fluctuations in these economic measures. The study reveals that the coupling structure of inflation and unemployment tends to Gaussian behavior after two years  indicating a complex interaction between these variables over different time scales.

The research contributes to the understanding of the theoretical complexity of inflation and unemployment  suggesting that these economic indicators exhibit multifractal nature and non-Gaussian probability density functions. This behavior may originate from the occurrence of large fluctuations in the system at extreme values. The findings have implications for policymakers  as understanding the coupling and non-Gaussianity of these variables can inform economic policies during periods of recession and other critical economic conditions.

Overall  the thesis provides a comprehensive analysis of the coupled criticality of inflation and unemployment  highlighting the importance of considering the complexity and non-Gaussianity of these economic indicators in macroeconomic analysis and policy-making.
